# Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval (CI) is the most useful single object in applied
statistics. It says: *"with method M, repeated over many studies, the
interval would cover the true parameter X% of the time."*

## CI for a Mean

For approximately normal data or large *n*:

$$\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

```r
x <- rnorm(40, mean = 100, sd = 15)
t.test(x)$conf.int               # 95% CI by default
t.test(x, conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
```

## CI for a Proportion

Use the Wilson interval (better than Wald, especially near 0 or 1):

```r
prop.test(47, 50)$conf.int
binom.test(47, 50)$conf.int
```

## The Bootstrap: When Theory Is Hard

The bootstrap [@efron1979bootstrap] constructs a sampling distribution by
resampling with replacement from your data. It is the workhorse for any
statistic without a clean analytical CI --- including the geometric mean, the
median, a ratio of medians, etc.

```r
library(boot)
speedups <- c(1.5, 2.0, 0.8, 3.0, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 0.9, 1.1, 1.6)

geo_mean <- function(d, i) exp(mean(log(d[i])))

b <- boot(speedups, geo_mean, R = 5000)
boot.ci(b, type = c("perc", "bca"))
```

`bca` (bias-corrected and accelerated) is generally the most accurate.

## Reporting

Always pair a point estimate with an interval:

> Mean latency was 12.4 ms (95% CI: 11.8–13.1, n = 30).

A point estimate without an interval is a half-truth.
